cells.tense: You are standing at the close of something and you know it is closing.
cells.ask: Finish one thing today and say out loud what it was for. Then leave the next thing undecided until tomorrow.
cells.core:
You can tell when something has run its course. Not because it failed — because it's done, and you can feel the done-ness without needing to keep it alive. That's rare. Most people either drag things past their end or drop them before they're finished.

The momentum you carry has a finish line in view, and you're not afraid of it. You're pointed at what's next, but you're not running from what's ending. The strength here is that you stay in the room while it closes. You don't need to declare the next chapter before this one has finished speaking. That steadiness is what makes the next thing clean when it arrives.
cells.sheetLine: You can let something end without rushing the next thing.
cells.verb: closing the loop and letting it open the next one
cells.place: in the room where momentum is aimed at a destination

cells.tense: You are already standing in a finish that has not happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing and leave it visibly unfinished today. No summary, no wrap-up. Let someone see it still in progress.
cells.core:
You've started calling things done before they're done. Not lying — anticipating. You can see the shape of the completed thing so clearly that you skip the part where it's still being made, and you describe it as finished while you're still inside it.

That jumping-ahead costs you the middle, which is where most of the actual work lives. People around you might be following a story you've already ended. The momentum is real and so is the direction. What's off is the timing. You're living in a version of this that hasn't arrived, and the version you're in hasn't gotten to finish becoming what it is.
cells.sheetLine: You've been calling things finished before they finish.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing sitting open. Say it's done — to one person, plainly. Then decide nothing about what comes after.
cells.core:
Nothing quite closes. Something gets almost there and then another angle opens, another version, another thing to try first — and the list of open loops keeps growing instead of shrinking. From inside it doesn't feel like stalling. It feels like thoroughness, or patience, or waiting for the right moment.

The momentum is there but it has nowhere to land. What's absent isn't effort. It's the willingness to say 'that one's over' and mean it. Every unfinished thing you carry is spending some of the energy that could be going into the one thing that's actually current. You don't have to finish everything. Close one and watch what frees up.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing closes, so nothing new can start clean.
cells.verb: closing the loop and letting it open the next one

cells.tense: You are already past a threshold you have not admitted you crossed.
cells.ask: Write down one thing that ended in the last year. Not what you learned — just that it ended. Keep it somewhere you'll see it.
cells.core:
You're moving with direction and you're not sure where the direction came from. Something shifted — a chapter closed, a way of working stopped, a version of things finished — and you kept walking as if it hadn't. The momentum is real. The accounting isn't.

This isn't about looking back for its own sake. It's that a finished thing you haven't marked is still pulling on you, quietly, as if it were open. You might be carrying weight from something that already set itself down. The release you're looking for isn't dramatic. It's just naming what's over so you stop spending energy on it.
cells.sheetLine: Something already ended. You're still carrying it as if it hadn't.

attempts.check: The record says the medicine for the Too Little cell is to charge the vertical twin (Compassion or its sibling), but it never names what that twin is or what action would charge it — I'm inferring the act from the seat's own description of focused motion, which the record supports loosely at best. A reader could reasonably say the Too Little cell describes avoidance when what's actually happening might be that the person hasn't yet found something worth finishing, not that they refuse to finish. The asks survive being wrong because each asks for one visible act with a finish, doable today, and teaches something about the person's relationship to cycles whether or not my read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're already the turning' — it flatters the reader's frame and says nothing the person could disagree with and still use.

A reader could say the Too Little person isn't refusing to finish anything, they just haven't landed on something worth finishing yet. The asks hold up either way: each is one visible act with a finish, doable today, and teaches the person how they relate to endings whether or not my read is right.
